**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Religious Studies 3 (0785), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Paper 3: The New Testament, Religion in Relation to Philosophy, Ethics and Morality, Historical Development of Islam (570CE-661CE). Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

The paper has six sections of six questions each: Section 2.1 The Gospel According to Luke (questions 1-6); Section 2.2 The Fourth Gospel (questions 7-12); Section 2.3 The Early Church as Reflected in Acts and 1 Corinthians (questions 13-18); Section 4.1 Philosophy of Religion (questions 19-24); Section 4.2 Ethics and Morality (questions 25-30); Section 6.0 The Historical Development of Islam (570CE - 661CE) (questions 31-36).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
What circumstances led to the historic battle of Badr?

(12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
According to Islamic tradition, the battle of Badr was fought in Ramadan in the second year after the Hijra (AD 624), and several circumstances led to it.

- *Persecution and loss of property.* For years the Quraysh of Mecca had persecuted the Muslims, and when the Muslims migrated to Medina in 622 many left their homes and property behind, which the Quraysh seized. The emigrants (Muhajirun) were poor, and they felt that they had a right to recover what had been taken from them.
- *The Meccan trade route.* The Quraysh lived by trade, and their caravans to Syria passed near Medina. After the Hijra the Muslims became a power that could threaten this trade, and the Muslim leadership saw that stopping the caravans could put pressure on Mecca to end its hostility. Small Muslim expeditions and raids were sent out in the months before Badr.
- *The great caravan of Abu Sufyan.* The Prophet learned that a large caravan, carrying much wealth and led by Abu Sufyan, was returning from Syria. He called the Muslims, about three hundred and thirteen men, to go out and intercept it. Not all expected a battle, and few animals and weapons were taken.
- *The Meccan army.* Abu Sufyan heard of the movement and changed his route toward the coast, and sent a message to Mecca for help. The Quraysh, led by Abu Jahl, raised an army of about a thousand, and even after the news that the caravan was safe they decided to go on to Badr, to defend their honour and to crush the Muslims.
- *The Muslim decision.* The Prophet consulted his companions, and the Muhajirun and Ansar both pledged support, and so the Muslims chose to confront the Quraysh at the wells of Badr.
- *Religious motivation.* Muslims regard the battle as a response to attack and as a test of faith; the Qur'an (in Surah al-Anfal) speaks of God's help given to the believers at Badr.

questions.enonce_markdown:
In which ways were its results of importance to Islam?

(13 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The results of Badr were of great importance for the young Muslim community. The figures differ slightly in the early sources, but according to tradition the Muslims, though much fewer in number, won a clear victory, about seventy Quraysh were killed and about seventy taken prisoner, while the Muslims lost about fourteen men.

- *Strengthening of faith and morale.* The Muslims regarded the victory as a sign of divine help, as the Qur'an describes. The victory greatly increased their confidence, and they called the day *Yawm al-Furqan*, the day of decision, in the light of the Qur'an.
- *Political and military standing.* Before Badr, the Muslims were a small group of emigrants and helpers in Medina. After it, they were a power to be respected in Arabia. Tribes began to take the Muslims seriously, and the authority of the Prophet in Medina became firmer.
- *Weakening of the Quraysh.* Several leading Meccan opponents, including Abu Jahl, were killed, and the prestige of Mecca suffered. Trade was threatened, and the Quraysh were determined to take revenge, leading to the battle of Uhud the next year.
- *Economic gain.* The spoils of war provided help for the poor emigrants. The disagreements over their division led to Qur'anic guidance on the matter, which shows how events shaped the Islamic law.
- *Treatment of prisoners.* The prisoners were ransomed, and tradition says that some who could read and write gained their freedom by teaching Muslims to do so, an early encouragement of learning.
- *Discipline and organisation.* The battle showed the value of unity and obedience under the leadership of the Prophet, and strengthened the bond between the Muhajirun and Ansar.
- *Encouragement to others.* Some people in Medina who had hesitated, and some who were hostile, were impressed or silenced, and the number of those who accepted Islam grew.

Badr is therefore remembered as the first great victory of Islam and a turning point which made the survival and later expansion of the community possible.
